If you are asking a web development company in Pune to build a WordPress site, the decision that will shape the next five years of that site is rarely the colour scheme. It is how the pages are built: with WordPress's own block editor (often called Gutenberg) and a block theme, or with a visual page builder such as Elementor, Divi or WPBakery. For most small and mid-sized business websites in 2026, the block editor with a well-made block theme is the safer default, because it is part of WordPress core, produces lighter pages and does not lock your content into one vendor's format. A page builder still makes sense in specific cases, mainly when non-technical staff need to design new landing pages often and the agency will keep the site lean. This guide explains how to make that choice, what each option costs you later, and the questions to put to any vendor before you sign.

It is written for business owners, marketing managers and founders who will own the site after launch, not for developers. Where we give time or cost figures they are ranges from typical projects, not quotes.

## What the two approaches actually are

### The block editor and block themes

Since WordPress 5.0 (December 2018), every page and post is edited in the block editor: paragraphs, headings, images, columns, buttons and so on are separate "blocks" you add and arrange. WordPress 5.9 (January 2022) extended the same idea to the whole site through block themes and the Site Editor, so headers, footers and page templates are also built from blocks rather than PHP template files a developer has to change.

In practice, a block-based build means:

- Content is stored as normal HTML with small comments that mark where each block starts and ends. If you switch themes, the text, headings and images remain readable.
- Design rules such as colours, fonts and spacing live in one place (a file called `theme.json`), so editors pick from a controlled palette rather than inventing new styles on every page.
- An agency can create **block patterns**, pre-designed sections such as "service hero", "three-step process" or "testimonial row", that your team inserts and edits without touching layout code.
- Custom blocks can be built for things only your business needs, such as a branch locator or a course schedule.

### Visual page builders

A page builder is a plugin that replaces or sits alongside the WordPress editor with its own drag-and-drop interface. Elementor is the best known; Divi, Beaver Builder, Bricks and WPBakery are others. They offer a large library of widgets (sliders, tabs, counters, forms, pop-ups), very fine control over spacing and responsive behaviour, and a live visual canvas that feels closer to Canva than to a word processor.

The trade-off is that the page layout is stored in the builder's own format. Elementor, for example, saves its layout data in its own fields; if the plugin is deactivated, pages typically fall back to a rough, unstyled version of the content, or in some builders to a wall of shortcodes. That is not a defect, it is how those tools work, but it matters when you think about ownership and future changes.

## The decision in one table

| Question | Block editor + block theme | Page builder (e.g. Elementor) |
|---|---|---|
| Who maintains it? | WordPress core team, updated with every release | The plugin vendor; Pro features need a paid licence |
| Licence cost | None for core; some block plugins have paid tiers | Free versions exist; Pro licences are an annual cost per site (check current pricing) |
| Page weight | Generally lighter: less extra CSS and JavaScript | Generally heavier unless carefully configured |
| Editor freedom | Controlled: patterns and locked styles | Very high: almost anything can be changed |
| Risk of inconsistent design | Lower | Higher, especially with many editors |
| Leaving the tool later | Content remains clean HTML | Layouts must usually be rebuilt |
| Learning curve for staff | Moderate; improves with good patterns | Low for simple edits, higher for advanced layouts |
| Developer skills needed | Modern WordPress (blocks, theme.json, some React for custom blocks) | Builder-specific knowledge; less code |

Neither column is "right". The table helps you see which risks you are choosing.

## Why this matters more than it looks: speed, Core Web Vitals and search

Google uses page experience signals, including the Core Web Vitals, as part of how it evaluates pages. Since March 2024 the responsiveness metric is Interaction to Next Paint (INP), which measures how quickly a page reacts when someone taps or clicks. Pages that load large amounts of JavaScript and CSS tend to struggle on INP and on Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), particularly on mid-range Android phones on mobile data, which is how a large share of Indian visitors arrive.

Page builders are not automatically slow. Recent versions of the major builders have added features such as loading only the CSS and scripts that a page uses, flexbox "containers" instead of nested sections, and optional removal of older libraries. A disciplined developer can build a fast Elementor site. The problem is that the defaults and the culture around builders push the other way: a slider here, an animation there, three fonts, a pop-up plugin, an add-on pack with forty widgets of which the site uses two. Each addition is small; together they produce pages that feel sluggish on a phone.

A block-theme site starts lighter because there is less on top of WordPress itself. It can of course be made slow too, with heavy images or careless plugins. We explain how to measure and fix responsiveness in our guide to [Interaction to Next Paint for business websites](/blog/web-development-company-pune-inp-interaction-to-next-paint-2026).

Two points to keep in proportion:

1. Speed is one ranking consideration among many. A fast page with thin content will not outrank a useful, slightly slower one. Better content and clear structure come first.
2. Speed affects people more directly than rankings. A visitor who taps "Call" or "WhatsApp" and waits is a visitor who may go back to the search results.

## Who edits the site after launch

This is the question we ask every client, and the answer often decides the build.

### Scenario A: you will edit text, prices and photos, not layouts

Most service businesses (clinics, consultants, coaching institutes, manufacturers, interior designers) change content far more often than layout. They update a price, add a new service, swap a photo, publish a blog post. For them, a block theme with a set of well-designed patterns is ideal. Editors cannot accidentally break the layout because the structure is locked, and new pages look consistent because they are assembled from the same approved sections.

### Scenario B: marketing builds new landing pages every month

A business that runs Google Ads or Meta campaigns with a new landing page for each offer has a different need. The marketing team wants to duplicate a page, rearrange sections, test a different headline and publish without waiting for a developer. A page builder can make that easy. The block editor can also do it with a good pattern library, and for many teams that is enough, but if your marketers are already fluent in a builder and the agency is disciplined about performance, a builder can be the pragmatic choice.

A middle path we often recommend: build the main site on blocks, and keep campaign landing pages on a small set of reusable landing-page patterns. If your campaigns need more, consider whether a separate landing-page tool is better than loading a builder across the whole site.

### Scenario C: several people, little supervision

Where many staff or branch managers edit the site, consistency matters more than freedom. Page builders give every editor control over fonts, colours and spacing, and over time the site drifts: one page with a bright red button, another with a different heading size. Block themes let the developer restrict which design options each user can change. For multi-author sites, that control is worth a lot.

## Cost: build, licences and the long tail

We are often asked whether a page builder makes a website cheaper. Sometimes it makes the first version faster to produce, especially for template-based sites. The longer-term costs are where the difference shows.

**Build cost.** For a typical 10 to 20 page business website, the build effort is broadly comparable between a competent block-theme build and a competent builder build, because most of the time goes into content, design decisions, responsive checks, forms, SEO setup and testing rather than into placing elements on a page. A custom block or two for special features adds development time. We do not quote a single figure here because the honest number depends on page count, features and who supplies the content; our [website creation services](/services/website-creation) page lists current packages, and any vendor should be able to show you the line items for either approach.

**Licences.** Core WordPress and its block editor cost nothing. Page builder Pro licences and add-on packs are annual subscriptions. They are not large for a single site, but they must be renewed for updates and security fixes, and someone must own the account. Ask who holds the licence: you or the agency.

**Maintenance.** Every plugin is something to update and something that can conflict with another plugin. A builder plus a third-party add-on pack adds two more moving parts. We cover how to judge plugins and spot abandoned ones in our [WordPress plugin audit guide](/blog/web-development-company-pune-wordpress-plugin-audit-abandoned-plugins-2026).

**Redesign.** The biggest hidden cost appears three or four years later when you want a new look. With a block theme, you can usually change the theme and restyle the existing patterns while the content stays in place. With a builder, each page's layout is tied to the builder; switching to something else typically means rebuilding pages one by one. Even a redesign within the same builder often means re-editing every page, because each page carries its own styling.

## Ownership and lock-in

Lock-in is not only a technical worry. It affects your negotiating position with agencies.

- If your site depends on an agency's private licence for a builder or a premium theme, you may lose updates when the relationship ends. Insist that licences are bought in your name or transferred at handover.
- If the agency has built custom blocks, ask for the source code and confirm in the agreement that you own it. Our [website handover and ownership checklist](/blog/web-development-company-pune-website-handover-ownership-checklist-2026) lists what to collect.
- If a builder is used, ask whether its free version can display your pages if the Pro licence lapses. In some builders, Pro widgets stop rendering properly without an active licence. Check the current behaviour with the vendor; it changes between versions.

## Accessibility

An accessible site is easier for everyone to use, and in India it is increasingly expected by government, CSR and large corporate buyers. The WCAG 2.2 guidelines from the W3C are the usual reference. Both approaches can produce accessible pages, but they fail in different ways:

- Builders make it easy to choose low-contrast colours, use headings for visual size rather than structure, and add carousels, tabs and pop-ups that are hard to use with a keyboard or screen reader unless configured carefully.
- Block themes are not automatically accessible either, but a locked palette and patterns designed once with proper heading order and contrast reduce the chance that later edits break things.

Whichever you choose, test with a keyboard (Tab, Enter, Esc) and an automated checker before launch, and fix headings so each page has one H1 and a sensible H2/H3 order.

## SEO and structured content

Neither approach is "better for SEO" in itself. What matters for search is the content, the internal linking, the page titles and meta descriptions, the speed, and structured data that describes your business and services accurately.

Two practical differences:

1. **Structured content.** If your site has repeated items such as services, branches, courses or projects, you will get more value from WordPress custom post types and fields than from either editor alone. A block theme combines naturally with that approach. We cover it in detail in our guide to [WordPress custom post types for service businesses](/blog/web-development-company-pune-wordpress-custom-post-types-structured-content-service-pages-2026).
2. **Clean markup.** Builders historically wrapped content in many nested `div` elements. Modern versions have improved, but a block theme still tends to produce simpler HTML, which is easier for assistive technology and a little easier for crawlers to parse. It is a small advantage, not a decisive one.

If you want help with titles, schema and internal links whichever editor you choose, see our [SEO services](/services/seo).

## When we would recommend a page builder

It would be dishonest to say page builders are always the wrong choice. We would consider one when:

- The client already has a team trained on a specific builder and a working set of templates, and the site is performing acceptably. Rebuilding for its own sake is not a good use of money.
- Campaign landing pages change weekly and the marketing team has no developer support.
- The design calls for complex, highly visual layouts on a small number of pages and the agency commits to a performance budget.
- The project is a short-lived microsite (an event or launch) where long-term maintenance is not a concern.

In each case we would still set rules: one builder only, no add-on packs unless a specific widget is required, a limited global palette and font set, and a page-weight target checked before launch.

## When we would recommend blocks

- A new business website expected to last several years.
- Sites with several editors or branches.
- Sites where speed on mobile matters, which is most sites whose visitors come from Google search or ads.
- Sites where you want to be able to change agencies without rebuilding.
- Content-heavy sites with a blog, resource library or many service pages.

## Migrating an existing builder site

Many Pune businesses already run an Elementor or WPBakery site from an earlier vendor and ask whether to move. Our advice:

1. **Measure first.** Run PageSpeed Insights on your top five landing pages and look at the field data (real visitors) where available, not just the lab score. Check INP and LCP on mobile.
2. **Count the pain.** How often do edits go wrong? How many plugins do you run? Are licences current and in your name?
3. **Consider a staged move.** Rebuild the highest-traffic templates (home, main service pages, contact) on blocks first; leave rarely visited pages until later.
4. **Protect search rankings.** Keep URLs the same, keep titles and on-page content, and check redirects for anything that changes. A redesign that changes URLs without a redirect map can lose traffic for months.
5. **Budget honestly.** Expect to rebuild layouts page by page. Content can usually be copied across; the visual structure cannot.

If the site is performing well and the team is comfortable, the right answer may be to stay and tidy up: remove unused add-ons, enable the builder's performance options, compress images and limit fonts.

## Questions to ask a web development company in Pune before you sign

1. Will you build with the block editor, a page builder or a mix? Why for our site specifically?
2. Who will hold any theme or builder licences, and in whose name?
3. What will our staff be able to change, and what is locked? Can you show us the editing screen for one of your past sites?
4. Will you create reusable patterns or templates for our common page sections?
5. What is your performance target for mobile, and how will you check it before launch?
6. How many plugins do you expect to install, and why each one?
7. If we move to another agency in three years, what will they inherit?
8. Do you provide training and a short written guide for editors?

A good vendor will answer these without jargon and will be happy to show you a real admin screen, not only the public site.

## How we approach it at Govindani Infotech

Our default for new business websites is the block editor with a custom block theme, a pattern library built around the client's real page types, and custom post types where the content repeats. We use page builders when a client's situation clearly calls for one, and we set performance and design limits when we do. If you are planning a new website or wondering whether to rebuild an existing one, see our [website creation services](/services/website-creation) or [contact us](/contact-us); you can also visit our office at Landmark Plaza, Satara Road, Pune, or call 092019 58274. We are happy to look at an existing site's admin and tell you plainly whether a rebuild is worth it.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is Elementor bad for SEO?
No. Elementor pages can rank well. The risk is that builder sites often become heavy, which can hurt loading speed and responsiveness on phones. With careful configuration, few add-ons and optimised images, an Elementor site can be fast; with defaults and many widgets, it usually is not.

### Is the WordPress block editor good enough for a business website in 2026?
Yes, for most business sites. Block themes, patterns and the Site Editor let an agency build a full custom design and give your team safe, consistent editing. Custom blocks cover anything specific to your business.

### Can I switch from Elementor to the block editor later?
Yes, but the page layouts usually have to be rebuilt, because the builder stores them in its own format. Text and images can be copied across. Plan a staged move, keep the same URLs and check redirects so you do not lose search traffic.

### Which is cheaper, a page builder or a block theme?
The first build costs are often similar for a typical business site. Over several years, block themes tend to cost less because there are no builder licences to renew, fewer plugins to maintain and redesigns do not require rebuilding every page.

### Can non-technical staff edit a block theme site?
Yes, if the developer provides reusable patterns and locks the design settings. Staff then edit text, images and buttons inside approved sections. Ask your vendor for a short training session and a written editing guide at handover.
